title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights into Reason-induced Misalignment
claim: Strengthening specific reasoning patterns raises misalignment versus controls, as the example reasoning traces associated with each pattern illustrate.
layout: 2 panels: grouped bar chart left, three stacked example text boxes right
description: The left panel is a grouped bar chart of misalignment rate (0–40%) for three reasoning patterns: Instruction Deviation, Confirmatory Reasoning and Heuristic Reliance. Each pattern has a light-blue Control bar and a dark-navy Target bar with percentage labels. Target bars reach about 31–35%, and control bars are about 22–25%. The right panel has three stacked rounded boxes with black title bars naming the patterns. Each box has two rows of quoted reasoning snippets. One row is tagged Math Reasoning and the other is tagged Safety Reasoning. The snippets show hesitation, guessing, confirmation bias and hasty completion. The eye goes first to the tall dark bars, then to the quoted examples.
caption: Left: Average misalignment rate with different reasoning patterns (controlled group for comparison) for all eight models. Results for eight individual models are in [ref]. Right: The responses from math (upper) and HEx-PHI (lower) dataset associated with the reasoning patterns.
abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.
